name: Good Key, Bad Key
description: There are $$$n$$$ chests. The $$$i$$$-th chest contains $$$a_i$$$ coins. You need to open all $$$n$$$ chests in order from chest $$$1$$$ to chest $$$n$$$. There are two types of keys you can use to open a chest: a good key, which costs $$$k$$$ coins to use; a bad key, which does not cost any coins, but will halve all the coins in each unopened chest, including the chest it is about to open . The halving operation will round down to the nearest integer for each chest halved. In other words using a bad key to open chest $$$i$$$ will do $$$a_i = \lfloor{\frac{a_i}{2}\rfloor}$$$, $$$a_{i+1} = \lfloor\frac{a_{i+1}}{2}\rfloor, \dots, a_n = \lfloor \frac{a_n}{2}\rfloor$$$; any key (both good and bad) breaks after a usage, that is, it is a one-time use. You need to use in total $$$n$$$ keys, one for each chest. Initially, you have no coins and no keys. If you want to use a good key, then you need to buy it. During the process, you are allowed to go into debt; for example, if you have $$$1$$$ coin, you are allowed to buy a good key worth $$$k=3$$$ coins, and your balance will become $$$-2$$$ coins. Find the maximum number of coins you can have after opening all $$$n$$$ chests in order from chest $$$1$$$ to chest $$$n$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 10^5$$$; $$$0 \leq k \leq 10^9$$$) — the number of chests and the cost of a good key respectively. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_i$$$ ($$$0 \leq a_i \leq 10^9$$$)  — the amount of coins in each chest. The sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case output a single integer  — the maximum number of coins you can obtain after opening the chests in order from chest $$$1$$$ to chest $$$n$$$. Please note, that the answer for some test cases won't fit into 32-bit integer type, so you should use at least 64-bit integer type in your programming language (like long long for C++).
approach_summary: Define state dp[mask][i] capturing the subset of visited/chosen elements. Transition by iterating over valid unset bits in O(2^N × N) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1703G — Good Key, Bad Key [450. Bitmask DP]
topic_editorial.summary: Bitmask DP state compression over subsets.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because the dimension $N$ is small ($N \le 20$), each subset of chosen or visited elements can be encoded compactly into a single bitmask integer $0 \le \text{mask} < 2^N$. The optimal substructure property guarantees that to extend a subset $\text{mask}$, we only need to know the current subset and optionally the last added element.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: State Definition
Define $dp[\text{mask}]$ (or $dp[\text{mask}][u]$ if the last visited element matters) as:
- $dp[\text{mask}] = $ the optimal value obtainable using the subset of elements represented by the bitmask $\text{mask}$.

### Step 2: Base Cases
- Initialize all DP states to a sentinel value (e.g. $\infty$ for minimization, or $-\infty$ for maximization).
- Base state: $dp[0] = 0$ (empty configuration has cost zero).

### Step 3: Recurrence Relation & Transitions
For every mask from $0$ to $2^N - 1$:
If the state $dp[\text{mask}]$ is reachable:
For every element $i \in [0, N-1]$ such that the $i$-th bit is NOT set in $\text{mask}$ ($(\text{mask} \mathbin{\&} (1 \ll i)) == 0$):
$$\text{next\_mask} = \text{mask} \mid (1 \ll i)$$
$$dp[\text{next\_mask}] = \text{opt}\big(dp[\text{next\_mask}], dp[\text{mask}] + \text{cost}(\text{mask}, i)\big)$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
The final answer is stored in $dp[(1 \ll N) - 1]$, which corresponds to all $N$ elements being chosen.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N \cdot N)$
  There are $2^N$ total bitmasks. From each mask, we iterate over at most $N$ possible next bits to transition. For $N = 20$, $2^{20} \cdot 20 \approx 2 \times 10^7$ operations, which easily runs in $\approx 0.15$ seconds.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N)$
  Storing the DP table for all $2^N$ configurations requires $2^{20} \times 8$ bytes $\approx 8\text{ MB}$ of memory, well below 256 MB.
